Prehistoric Art
Semester 1 · 2 weeks · about 250 minutes per week
ESSENTIAL QUESTION
Why did human beings begin making art before they had writing, cities, or farming, and how do we read works whose makers left no words?

The oldest art we know is tens of thousands of years old. In this unit you meet the painters of the Lascaux caves, the carvers of the Venus figures, and the builders of Stonehenge. With no written record to lean on, you will rely on the tools from Unit 1: careful description, analysis of how each work is made, and interpretation held honestly as theory rather than fact.

What does a civilization build tallest and most carefully, and what does that choice reveal about what it holds highest?

The first cities on earth grew up along two great river systems: the Tigris and Euphrates in Mesopotamia, and the Nile in Egypt. Both built on a colossal scale, but for opposite reasons. Ancient Greece
Semester 1 · 3 weeks · about 250 minutes per week
ESSENTIAL QUESTION
What changed when artists began trying to show the human body and world as they truly appear?

In about four centuries, Greek artists moved from stiff, Egyptian-style figures to bodies caught in motion, and built temples of near-perfect proportion. This unit follows that breakthrough through sculpture, the Parthenon, and the stories painted on Greek pottery, the birth of naturalism in Western art.

Teacher Guide — Semester 1 Culminating Project: Virtual Museum Exhibit

Art History & Criticism 1 Honors (0100330)

Teacher-facing only. No benchmark codes, answer keys, or tier labels on student pages.

What it is

The semester capstone. Students become curators: select 5 to 7 works from Units 1 to 6, organize them around a theme, write museum labels (DAIJ-based), and present a digital exhibit. Major project, 100 points (the Map weights Major Projects & Assessments at 60% of the grade).

Files

  • cp1-00-virtual-museum-guide.html — interactive Project Guide (Tier 4 scaffolding, GitHub-deployed): what a curator does, choosing works, writing labels (with a wall-label-anatomy visual), building and presenting in PowerPoint, optional VR gallery. Engine: reflect + select.
  • CP1-01-virtual-museum-exhibit-assignment.html — Canvas-native graded assignment (Tier 3): requirements, full M365 PowerPoint Skill Step, 4-criterion rubric, citation requirement, optional VR enrichment.

Tier / load

This is the unit's single Tier-3 teacher-graded assessment for the cycle (it replaces a normal unit's analysis essay as the big grading event). Rubric is 4 criteria, kept consistent with the course's other rubrics in spirit. Budget ~5 min/student at the slide level.

Standards alignment

VA.912.F.1.5 (digital presentation analyzing/comparing artists and works in historical context) is the anchor; also F.2.8 (exhibit/preserve art), F.3.5 (cited sources), C.1.4, H.1.4, C.3.5 (cross-cultural/timeline connections), and ELA.K12.EE.1.1 / EE.5.1 (evidence; format conventions). Texas (TEKS §117.302), added 2026-07-13: the guide's careers panel carries 3(D) (career vs. avocational opportunities in art); the class gallery walk + docent comments carry 3(C) (community-based art project) and, with the live-section partner option, 2(E) (collaborative artmaking).

Class gallery walk (added 2026-07-13; how to run it)

After the due date, assemble the exhibits into a shared class gallery: a VR gallery of slide exports, a shared compilation deck, or simply a Canvas discussion where each student posts their exhibit file or link. Students visit at least two classmates' exhibits and leave one docent comment each (something the curation helped them see). Lowest-lift build: a Canvas Discussion "CP1 Gallery Walk" where posting your exhibit + two docent comments = completion credit under Reflections/Discussions/Participation. Budget ~0 grading time (completion scan). Live sections may offer the partner-exhibit option printed on the assignment (8 to 10 works, both names on the title slide, each partner labels their own works); grade partners on the same rubric, one submission.

Deliverable & M365

PowerPoint (.pptx), Band C: single design theme, file named LastName_FirstName_MuseumExhibit_AHC1H, saved to the course OneDrive folder, submitted via the Canvas OneDrive tab. Micro-cert moment: Apply a Slide Master / Design Theme (PowerPoint).

Notes

  • Students must use only PD/CC images (course Artwork Image Banks or the approved source list) and cite each; in-copyright works are linked, not reproduced.
  • The Unit 6 outro survey (Q5) seeds this project by asking which work each student would feature.
  • The optional VR gallery is platform-agnostic (place images on a wall, add labels, capture a walkthrough); it does not replace the PowerPoint.

Teacher Guide — Art History & Criticism 1 Honors (0100330)

Sample Build: Units 1 & 2

Course: Art History and Criticism 1 Honors · CPALMS #0100330 · Grades 9–12 · Honors · 1 credit · Year-long · Performing/Fine Arts graduation credit. Async model: Self-paced in Canvas with a live teacher (office hours, email, grading). Live VR sections use the same curriculum unchanged. Budget: ~250 minutes/week (M–F). Teacher-facing only — do not expose benchmark codes, answer keys, or tier labels to students.

1. How the pieces deploy

  • Interactive lessons (/interactive-lessons/*.html) — full HTML documents hosted on GitHub Pages, embedded in Canvas via iframe. Widgets and the images/ folder travel with them. (See canvas-interactive-widgets.)
  • Canvas-native items (/canvas-native/*.html) — inline-styled fragments pasted into the Canvas RCE (pages, assignment descriptions). No <style>/<script>.
  • Quizzes — built in Canvas from the *-quiz-SPEC.md files (auto-graded; answer keys below).
  • Artwork Image Bank — upload the public-domain images in /interactive-lessons/images/ to a Canvas module file set students can open; each is credited there.

2. Teacher grading load (per the 500:1 model)

Item Tier Grading

Design Challenge, Symbol Painting T1 Completion + effort
Unit Quizzes T1 Auto-graded

Honors rigor: emphasis on analysis, evidence-based judgment, and held-open interpretation (Honors note in CPALMS).

4. Quiz answer keys

See U1-06-quiz-SPEC.md and U2-06-quiz-SPEC.md — correct options marked with ✅. Enter into Canvas with answer shuffling on. Do not post these keys to students.

5. Artwork image bank — copyright status & VERIFY notes

All featured works are public-domain artworks (centuries pre-1928). Per OAO Copyright Policy §3.2, a single image used in full for educational analysis is permitted with creator/source citation.

6. Looking ahead — copyright flags for later units

  • Unit 11 (Modern & Contemporary): Fauvism, Dada, Surrealism, Abstract Expressionism, Pop, Minimalism are in copyright and must be linked out to the holding museum (MoMA, Tate), never embedded. The source art folder correctly contains no Modern/Contemporary images.
  • Sourcing gaps to fill from approved PD/CC sources: Parthenon + a Greek narrative vase (U4), Augustus of Prima Porta (U5, optional alt = Colosseum), Islamic works such as the Dome of the Rock / Great Mosque of Córdoba (U6).

7. Module wrappers & analytics

Intro/outro pages may be built as ungraded Canvas surveys (a single completion question) if you want module-completion analytics; otherwise use them as plain Pages. Keep the navy/cyan header byte-consistent across all items.

8. Required syllabus/Canvas copyright disclosure (Policy §8.1/§8.2)

Include in the syllabus and course shell: "Optima Academy Online course materials are original instructional materials. Artworks are reproduced only where in the public domain or used as a limited fair-use excerpt for educational analysis, with sources cited; works under copyright are linked to the holding institution rather than reproduced."

VR journal: teacher note (moved off the student page)

Students complete this alone in one headset session. Common sticking points: finding the placed-note or annotation tool, and over-claiming in the Interpret step. Encourage students to tie interpretation to what they can see, and to keep the visit to about 30 minutes. In a live setting, invite students to compare what struck each of them after the visit; the curriculum does not require it, but the moment is worth taking.

assignments.title: Formal Analysis of a Selected Artwork
assignments.html:
ART HISTORY & CRITICISM · UNIT 1 · ANALYSIS ASSIGNMENT
Formal Analysis of a Selected Artwork
Points: 40  ·  Submit: one Word document (.docx)  ·  Due: end of Week 1

Now you put the DAIJ method to work on your own. Choose one artwork from the list below. At the top of your Word document, write the title, artist, and date of the work you chose so your reader knows exactly which artwork you are analyzing. Then write a complete four-part analysis of it. This is the move you will repeat, on harder works, all year, so look first and write second.

The School of Athens, Raphael (Raffaello Sanzio), 1509 to 1511. Fresco, Stanza della Segnatura, Apostolic Palace, Vatican City. Public domain.
🎨 CHOOSE ONE ARTWORK (all are in the public domain; each is embedded in the module Artwork Image Bank with full citation)
• The School of Athens, Raphael, 1509 to 1511 (Vatican)
• Impression, Sunrise, Claude Monet, 1872 (Musée Marmottan Monet, Paris)
• Oath of the Horatii, Jacques-Louis David, 1784 (Louvre, Paris)
• The Calling of Saint Matthew, Caravaggio, 1599 to 1600 (San Luigi dei Francesi, Rome)
• The Raft of the Medusa, Théodore Géricault, 1819 (Louvre, Paris)
📝 WRITE ONE SHORT PARAGRAPH FOR EACH STEP
D · Describe. What do you see? The subject, figures, objects, and setting. Only what is literally there.

A · Analyze. How is it organized? Name two or three Elements of Art or Principles of Design that drive the work, and explain how each one functions. Precision beats coverage.

I · Interpret. What is the artist trying to say? Every claim must point back to something in your Describe or Analyze.

J · Judge. Does the work succeed at what it set out to do, and how do you know? Build your verdict on the three steps above.
📁 M365 SKILL STEP
Before submitting, make sure you have:
☐ Opened Microsoft Word from your school Microsoft 365 account
☐ Named your file: LastName_FirstName_FormalAnalysis_AHC1H
☐ Saved it to your Optima › Art › ArtHistory_2026-27 OneDrive folder
☐ Submitted through Canvas using the OneDrive tab
M365 Skill You’re Practicing: Insert Citations & build a Works Cited (Word) · cite the artwork and any source you consult. New to OneDrive? See the M365 Setup & File Organization Guide.
⚠️ WORTH KNOWING · THIS IS YOUR OWN LOOKING
An AI tool can generate a polished-sounding analysis in seconds, but it often invents details that are not in the painting and cannot verify its claims against the actual image. This assignment grades your eye: your ability to point to what is really there. Write from your own observation.
✅ HOW YOU WILL BE GRADED (40 points)
CriterionPoints
Describe: accurate, specific, observation only10
Analyze: names 2 to 3 Elements/Principles and how they work10
Interpret: meaning tied to visual evidence10
Judge and use of vocabulary: reasoned verdict, correct art terms10

Elements & Principles Design Challenge

You have learned to spot the Elements of Art and Principles of Design in great works. Now use them on purpose. assignments.html:
ART HISTORY & CRITICISM · UNIT 2 · ANALYSIS ASSIGNMENT
Lascaux Cave Painting Analysis
Points: 40  ·  Submit: one Word document (.docx)  ·  Due: end of Week 1

Write a full four-step analysis of the Lascaux painting below. Because the painters left no written record, your Describe and Analyze steps carry the most weight, and your Interpret step must be offered as a careful theory.

Cave paintings of aurochs, horses, and deer, Lascaux, c. 17,300 years old (Upper Paleolithic). Dordogne, France. Photograph by Prof saxx, 2006, licensed under CC BY-SA 3.0. Retrieved from Wikimedia Commons.
📝 WRITE ONE PARAGRAPH PER STEP
D · Describe. What animal do you see? What pose, what direction, what details? Only what is literally there.

A · Analyze. Name two or three Elements of Art the painter used (consider line, form, color, space) and explain how. Mention the technique: natural earth pigments, use of the rock’s shape.

I · Interpret. Begin with “One possible reading is…” Offer a theory of purpose (ritual, hunting magic, record-keeping) and tie it to evidence such as the cave’s deep placement.

J · Judge. As a work of image-making, how skillful is it? Defend your verdict from your description and analysis.
📁 M365 REMINDER
Write in Microsoft Word (Microsoft 365). Name your file LastName_FirstName_LascauxAnalysis_AHC1H, save it to your Optima › Art › ArtHistory_2026-27 OneDrive folder, and submit through the Canvas OneDrive tab. Target length: about one page (300 to 450 words).

⚠️ WORTH KNOWING · KEEP THE QUESTION OPEN
If you ask an AI tool what these paintings “mean,” it will likely give one confident answer. Scholars genuinely disagree. Your Interpret step is stronger, not weaker, when it names a theory as a theory and admits what we cannot know.
✅ HOW YOU WILL BE GRADED (40 points)
CriterionPoints
Describe: accurate, observation only10
Analyze: Elements + technique, explained10
Interpret: theory tied to evidence, honestly framed10
Judge and vocabulary: reasoned, correct terms10

Prehistoric Symbol Painting
Points: 20 (completion + effort)  ·  Submit: a photo (JPG/PNG) and a 2 to 3 sentence note

The first artists worked with the materials of the earth, a limited palette, and powerful, simple imagery. You will work the same way. • an earth-tone palette (browns, reds, ochres, black, charcoal; pencil, crayon, marker, paint, even coffee or dirt if you like)
• simple symbols and outlined shapes, the way prehistoric painters reduced an animal to its essential lines
• no realistic detail and no words

📝 ARTIST’S NOTE (write in the submission box)

ART HISTORY & CRITICISM · UNIT 2 · VR MUSEUM JOURNAL
Standing Among the First Works
Points: 20 (completion)  ·  Submit: your journal answers (text entry) + one screenshot

What you are doing. Scale changes how a work feels. A cave painting on a screen is one thing; standing beneath an animal painted larger than life, or among stones twice your height, is another. In the virtual environment you can experience prehistoric works at something closer to their real presence. You will visit two settings and keep a short journal as you go.

🧭 WHAT YOU NEED & HOW TO BEGIN
A VR headset (or the desktop option if that is what you have). Open the Unit 2 virtual experience from the course VR area, and have your lesson vocabulary handy. You will visit a cave-painting space and a standing-stone monument. Where a setting offers a choice of viewing spot, choose wherever you can see the work best.
👀 PART 1 · LOOK & RECORD (in the cave-painting space)
1. Stand close, then step back. What changes about the painting when you move? (1 to 2 sentences)
2. Describe one animal exactly as you see it from where you stand.
3. Analyze: name one Element of Art that is more powerful at this scale than it was on the screen, and say why.
👀 PART 2 · LOOK & RECORD (at the standing-stone monument)
4. Walk around the stones. Find a trilithon and describe what makes it post-and-lintel construction.
5. Interpret: standing inside the circle, what does the space feel built for? Begin with “One possible reading is…”

ART HISTORY & CRITICISM · UNIT 3 · CREATION ACTIVITY
Egyptian Cartouche Design
Points: 20 (completion + effort)  ·  Submit: a photo (JPG/PNG) and a 2 to 3 sentence note

In Egyptian art, a royal name was written in symbols and enclosed in an oval loop called a cartouche, which set the name apart as important and protected. You will design your own. This is a variation exercise: you take a genuine Egyptian convention and apply it to your own name, using the design rules you studied.

✏️ YOUR TASK
On paper, draw a tall oval cartouche with a bar across one end (the Egyptian style). Inside it, design a symbol for each letter or sound of your first name. You invent the symbols, but follow real Egyptian habits:
• use clear, flat, outlined shapes a viewer could recognize
• stack or line them up in an orderly column or row (like a register)
• keep the design bold and readable, not realistic

Add color with an earth-tone palette if you wish. Sign your work.

Make it a print (optional): Egyptian seals stamped a name again and again. If you would like to work the same way, carve or press your finished design into a foam sheet, a produce tray, or thick cardboard, coat it with marker or paint, and press it onto paper to pull a relief print. Try two or three pulls and submit your best one.
📝 ARTIST’S NOTE (write in the submission box)

assignments.html:
ART HISTORY & CRITICISM · UNIT 5 · CREATION ACTIVITY
Roman Mosaic Design
Points: 20 (completion + effort)  ·  Submit: a photo (JPG/PNG) and a 2 to 3 sentence note

Romans built durable pictures one small tile at a time. You will do the same, on paper or on screen. This is a variation exercise: you take the real mosaic method, building an image from a grid of single-color units, and apply it to a subject of your own.

✏️ YOUR TASK
On graph paper, on a grid you draw (at least 15 by 15 squares), or on a digital grid if you prefer, design a mosaic of a single clear subject: an animal, a plant, a symbol, a letter. Follow the real method:
• fill whole squares with color, never partial squares (each square is one tessera)
• use a limited color palette, as Roman makers did with stone and glass
• add a simple repeating pattern border around your image
• keep the subject readable from a few steps back

Color it in by hand with markers, colored pencils, or paint, or build it in any digital tool you like, such as a spreadsheet with colored cells, a pixel-art app, or a drawing program. Sign your work.

Make it a relief (optional): Roman tesserae were real objects with real thickness. If you would like to work the same way, build your mosaic from small cut squares of colored paper or cardboard glued to a base, or press small tiles of modeling clay or salt dough into place. Keep the whole-square rule: one piece, one color.

discussions.title: Two Ways of Seeing
discussions.html:
Art history and art criticism ask different questions of the same work, and a good scholar uses both.

Post (by midweek): Choose one artwork from Lesson 1.01 or 1.02. Make one specific claim about it that belongs to art criticism (something you can only answer by looking hard at the work itself), and one specific claim that belongs to art history (something you would answer by research). State each claim in a full sentence and explain, in 4 to 6 sentences total, how the two kinds of questions would sharpen each other for that work.

Reply (by end of week): Respond to one classmate. Do you agree that their two claims land in the right discipline? If yes, strengthen one of them with an additional reason. If not, explain respectfully where you think the line falls and why.

Success criteria

  • Full credit: a specific criticism claim and a specific history claim, correctly sorted, with a clear explanation of how they connect; plus a substantive reply that adds reasoning.
  • Partial: claims present but vague, miscategorized, or reply is thin ("I agree").
  • Zero: missing.

discussions.title: Two Works, One Question
discussions.html:
A cave painting and a ring of standing stones could hardly look more different, yet an art historian can ask the same question of both: what does this work reveal about what its makers valued?

Post (by midweek): In 5 to 7 sentences, make one clear claim about what the Lascaux paintings suggest their makers valued, and one clear claim about what Stonehenge suggests its makers valued. Support each claim with something you can actually point to in the work (its placement, materials, scale, subject, or alignment). End by naming one real similarity between the two cultures’ priorities.

Reply (by end of week): Respond to one classmate. Does their evidence actually support their claim? If yes, add one more piece of evidence that strengthens it. If not, suggest, respectfully, what evidence would make the claim stronger.

Success criteria

  • Full credit: evidence-based claims about both works, a genuine similarity, and a substantive reply that engages a classmate’s evidence.
  • Partial: claims present but thinly supported, or a reply that only agrees without adding anything.
  • Zero: missing.

discussions.title: Two Rivers, Two Ways to Build
discussions.html:
Mesopotamia and Egypt both built on a colossal scale, but for opposite reasons. An art historian can compare them feature by feature.

Post (by midweek): In 5 to 7 sentences, compare the ziggurat and the Egyptian pyramid on at least three points: their material, their purpose, and the feeling their form creates. Support each point with something specific you can see or know about the works. End with one claim: what does each civilization’s greatest building reveal about what it valued most?

Reply (by end of week): Respond to one classmate. Does their evidence support their claim? If yes, add one more contrast they did not mention. If not, suggest, respectfully, what evidence would strengthen it.

Success criteria

  • Full credit: at least three well-supported contrasts, an evidence-based claim about each culture’s values, and a substantive reply.
  • Partial: contrasts present but thin or unsupported, or a reply that only agrees.
  • Zero: missing.

discussions.title: Two Ways to Carve a Person
discussions.html:
The Archaic Greek kouros and the Egyptian figure look surprisingly alike, which is no accident. But Greek sculpture then changed dramatically, while Egyptian art held steady.

Post (by midweek): In 5 to 7 sentences, compare the Egyptian standing figure (from Unit 3) with Greek sculpture. Name at least one clear similarity between the Egyptian figure and the early Archaic kouros, and explain why they resemble each other. Then name at least two ways Greek sculpture broke away (for example, contrapposto, naturalism, motion), pointing to a specific work. End with a claim: what did each culture seem to want its sculpture to do?

Reply (by end of week): Respond to one classmate. Does their evidence support their claim? If yes, add one more contrast or similarity. If not, suggest, respectfully, what would strengthen it.

Success criteria

  • Full credit: a well-explained similarity, at least two specific breakaways, an evidence-based claim about each culture’s aims, and a substantive reply.
  • Partial: points present but thin or unsupported, or a reply that only agrees.
  • Zero: missing.

discussions.title: Beauty or Power?
discussions.html:
It is often said that Greek art pursued ideal beauty while Roman art pursued power and use. Like all neat sayings, it is partly true and partly too simple.

Post (by midweek): In 5 to 7 sentences, compare Greek and Roman art and architecture on at least two points (for example: temple vs. amphitheater, idealized vs. veristic portraits, post-and-lintel vs. the arch). For each point, say what each culture seems to value. Then take a position: is the “beauty vs. power” contrast fair, or does it miss something? Support your view with a specific work.

Reply (by end of week): Respond to one classmate. Does the evidence fit their claim? Strengthen it with another example, or respectfully complicate it (for instance, by noting that Rome borrowed Greek beauty for the Augustus).

Success criteria

  • Full credit: at least two well-supported contrasts, a clear position on the saying, a specific work cited, and a substantive reply.
  • Partial: points present but thin, or a reply that only agrees.
  • Zero: missing.

discussions.title: Two Roads to the Sacred
discussions.html:
Byzantine and Gothic art are both Christian, both built to lift the worshiper toward God, yet they look and feel very different.

Post (by midweek): In 5 to 7 sentences, compare the Byzantine and Gothic approaches on at least two points (for example: gold mosaic vs. stained glass, the floating dome vs. the soaring vertical, flat sacred figures vs. light-filled space). For each, say what feeling the tradition was reaching for. Then take a position: do they pursue the same goal by different means, or genuinely different goals?

Reply (by end of week): Respond to one classmate. Add one more point of contrast or similarity, or respectfully complicate their position with a specific feature of Hagia Sophia or a Gothic cathedral.

Success criteria

  • Full credit: at least two well-supported contrasts, a clear position, specific works cited, and a substantive reply.
  • Partial: points present but thin, or a reply that only agrees.
  • Zero: missing.
